---
title: "Smoothing"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using ConvolutionInterpolations, CairoMakie, Printf, Random
rms(v) = sqrt(sum(abs2, v) / length(v));                   # root mean square, used throughout
```

Interpolation passes through the data; for measured data with noise that is not always what
you want. The Julia package smooths gridded data in two ways. `fit_scattered` fits a convolution
interpolant to the data with a roughness penalty whose weight is chosen by generalized
cross-validation, so nothing has to be tuned, and it reports the noise level it found. A
Gaussian kernel, in `convolution_smooth` and `convolution_gaussian`, averages the data with a
width you choose; it is a few separable passes over the data, orders of magnitude cheaper, and
the only feasible choice in many dimensions.

The Python port does not include smoothing yet; the [feature matrix](../features.qmd) tracks
the port.

## Smoothing with the parameter chosen for you

Gridded data are points that happen to lie on a grid, so they can be handed to the
scattered-data fit of the [scattered-data page](scattered.qmd) as a matrix of coordinates, one
column per point. A noisy sine:

```{julia}
Random.seed!(1)                                           # reproducible noise
x = range(0, 2π, length = 400)                            # a uniform grid
clean = sin.(x)                                           # the signal
noisy = clean .+ 0.1 .* randn(400)                        # the signal with noise of standard deviation 0.1

pts = reshape(collect(x), 1, :)                           # the knots as a 1 × n matrix of points
knots, vals, info = fit_scattered(pts, noisy)             # the fitted grid, with λ chosen by cross-validation
fit = convolution_interpolation(knots, vals; kernel = :a4, bc = :poly)   # the interpolant, with the kernel the fit used
info                                                      # the smoothing parameter and the estimated noise
```

```{julia}
xf = range(0, 2π, length = 1000)                          # fine points for plotting
fig = Figure(size = (800, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x")
scatter!(ax, x, noisy; markersize = 5, color = :white, strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1, label = "noisy data")
lines!(ax, xf, fit.(xf); label = "fitted interpolant")    # the fit, evaluated between the knots
lines!(ax, xf, sin.(xf); color = :black, label = "signal")   # the signal it was recovering
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | noisy data | fitted interpolant |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| rms error against the signal | %.4f | %.4f |\n", rms(noisy .- clean), rms(fit.(x) .- clean))
@printf("\nThe noise standard deviation estimated by the fit is %.4f; the noise was generated with 0.1.\n", info.noise)
```

The result is an interpolant, so derivatives and integrals of the smoothed signal come from the
same object, as on the other pages. The fit starts on a grid as fine as the data density
allows, so that nothing the points resolve is lost before the smoothing is chosen, and then
refits on the coarsest grid that resolves the smoothing it found — the grid it returns — and it
warns, pointing at the `oversample` keyword, when the fitted smoothing would need a finer grid
than the data allow. It solves a sparse system, so it costs more than a pass over the data,
and the system grows with the dimension.

The same fit on the same noise, with the signal's frequency raised, shows what the
cross-validation does: the smoothing follows the signal, not a preset width.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The fit at several signal frequencies"
ks = (1, 3, 10, 30)                                       # cycles over the interval
fit_errors = map(ks) do k
    cleank = sin.(k .* x)                                 # the signal at this frequency
    Random.seed!(1)
    noisyk = cleank .+ 0.1 .* randn(400)                  # the same noise realisation
    kn, vl, _ = fit_scattered(pts, noisyk)
    rms(convolution_interpolation(kn, vl; kernel = :a4, bc = :poly).(x) .- cleank)
end;
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| cycles over the interval | ", join(ks, " | "), " |")
println("|:--|", "--:|"^length(ks))
println("| rms error of the fit | ", join((@sprintf("%.4f", e) for e in fit_errors), " | "), " |")
```

## Gaussian smoothing

The Gaussian kernel has a single parameter `B`, the width in units of the grid spacing: the
weight of a neighbour $k$ spacings away is proportional to $\exp(-B k^2)$. So a larger `B` is a
narrower kernel and less smoothing; a smaller `B` is a wider kernel and more smoothing. The
weights are normalised to sum to one, so the mean level of the data is preserved. Around
`B ≈ 0.1` the result is usually good, and the optimum is shallow, so precise tuning rarely pays.
The same noisy sine, smoothed on the grid at a range of widths:

```{julia}
smoothed_01 = convolution_smooth(x, noisy, 0.1);           # smoothed values on the grid, B = 0.1
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
Bs = (2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01)
println("| B | ", join(Bs, " | "), " |")
println("|:--|", "--:|"^length(Bs))
println("| rms error after smoothing | ", join((@sprintf("%.4f", rms(convolution_smooth(x, noisy, B) .- clean)) for B in Bs), " | "), " |")
```

Too narrow a kernel leaves the noise; too wide a kernel flattens the peaks of the signal. The
table shows the shallow optimum between the two — and, against the fit's table above, that the
best `B` lands a little behind the fit, which was not told the width. A single width also
cannot follow a signal whose frequency changes across the data, where the fit's roughness
penalty can.

### In more dimensions

The Gaussian smoothing is separable, one axis at a time, so it costs about the same per value
in any number of dimensions:

```{julia}
Random.seed!(2)
xs = range(0, 2π, length = 150)                           # the grid along x
ys = range(0, 2π, length = 150)                           # the grid along y
field = [cos(xi) * sin(yi) for xi in xs, yi in ys]        # the signal
noisy2 = field .+ 0.2 .* randn(150, 150)                  # with noise

smoothed = convolution_smooth((xs, ys), noisy2, 0.1)      # smoothed values on the grid

fig = Figure(size = (800, 760))
for (pos, z, name) in ((fig[1, 1], noisy2, "noisy"), (fig[1, 2], smoothed, "smoothed, B = 0.1"), (fig[2, 1:2], field, "signal"))
    ax = Axis(pos; title = name, aspect = DataAspect())
    heatmap!(ax, xs, ys, z; colorrange = (-1.2, 1.2))
end
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | noisy | smoothed |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| rms error | %.4f | %.4f |\n", rms(noisy2 .- field), rms(smoothed .- field))
```

### Evaluating between the knots

`convolution_gaussian` builds the same smoothing as an interpolant, so it can be evaluated at
any point, not only on the grid. Between the knots the Gaussian weights sum to slightly less
than one, and the sum deviates more the narrower the kernel; up to `B = 0.34` the deviation is
below $10^{-12}$, which is why `convolution_gaussian` accepts `B` up to that value only, while
`convolution_smooth`, which evaluates on the knots, takes any `B`.

```{julia}
itp = convolution_gaussian(x, noisy, 0.1)                 # the smoothing as an interpolant
itp(1.5), itp.(x[1:3])                                    # anywhere, or on the knots
```

On the knots it agrees with `convolution_smooth`:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
@printf("The largest difference on the knots is %.2e.\n", maximum(abs.(itp.(x) .- convolution_smooth(x, noisy, 0.1))))
```

## Which to use

- The fit, when the result matters more than the time: it chooses the smoothing, estimates the
  noise, follows the signal's own scale, and returns an interpolant. Its cost grows with the
  grid and the dimension.
- The Gaussian, when the data are large or high-dimensional, or when the width is known. It is
  a few microseconds per thousand values, in any number of dimensions.

Both lose some accuracy near the boundaries, where the ghost values are extrapolated from noisy
data; that is a property of any local method, not of the kernel. The
[smoothing benchmark](../benchmarks/julia/smoothing.qmd) compares both with the alternatives, in
accuracy and in time, across noise levels and signal frequencies.
